rejected.title: Electron diffraction
card: Diffraction is the spreading of a wave as it passes through a gap or past an edge. Waves from neighbouring gaps overlap and make a pattern of bright and dark regions.
A crystal has atoms in regular rows. The rows act like a grating that can diffract electrons whose wavelength is close to the atom spacing.
The amount of spreading depends on the wavelength, not on how many electrons arrive. If the wavelength is much smaller than the spacing, the spread is too small to see.
When electrons pass through a thin crystal, they land on a screen in rings or spots, not one blob. Only waves make this pattern, which confirmed de Broglie's idea that electrons have a wavelength.
rejected.remember: A diffraction pattern from electrons shows they behave as waves.

a.q: A beam of electrons passes through a thin crystal and forms rings on a screen. What does this show?
opts: Electrons behave as waves
Electrons behave as tiny particles
Electrons turn into photons in the crystal
The crystal's atoms are not in regular rows
a.why: Rings come from waves spreading and overlapping, so the electrons behave as waves. Particles alone would not make rings, and it is the electrons, not light, that land in the pattern. The regular rows of atoms are what make the pattern possible.
a.clue: Which kind of model makes bright and dark patterns?

b.q: Nina fires electrons at a thin crystal and sees only a single bright spot straight ahead, with no rings. She expected rings. Which change would most likely bring the rings back?
opts: Using electrons with a wavelength near the atom spacing
Using electrons with a much shorter wavelength
Making the beam brighter with more electrons
Firing the same electrons at a slower rate
b.why: The crystal can diffract electrons clearly when their wavelength is close to the spacing of its atoms. A much shorter wavelength spreads even less, so the rings would stay too small to see. Changing how many electrons arrive, or how often, does not change how much they spread.
b.clue: What does the amount of spreading depend on?

draft.title: Electron diffraction
card: Diffraction is the spreading of a wave as it passes through a gap or past an edge. Waves from neighbouring gaps overlap and make a pattern of bright and dark regions.
A crystal has atoms in regular rows, with spacings close to the size of an electron's wavelength. The rows act like a grating that can diffract the electrons.
When a beam of electrons passes through a thin crystal, the electrons land on a screen in rings or spots, not as one blob. Only waves make this kind of pattern.
This confirmed de Broglie's idea that electrons have a wavelength. The pattern's spacing gives the wavelength, and it matches λ = h/p.
draft.remember: A diffraction pattern from electrons shows they behave as waves.

a.q: A beam of electrons passes through a thin crystal and forms rings on a screen. What does this show?
opts: Electrons can behave as waves
Electrons are heavier than atoms
Electrons carry no electric charge
Electrons travel faster than light
a.why: Rings come from waves overlapping after passing the crystal, so the electrons behave as waves. Mass, charge and speed do not make a diffraction pattern, so they cannot explain the rings.
a.clue: Which kind of model makes bright and dark patterns?

b.q: Nina fires electrons at a thin crystal and sees only a single bright spot straight ahead, with no rings. She expected rings. Which change would most likely bring the rings back?
opts: Using electrons with a wavelength near the atom spacing
Using electrons with a much shorter wavelength
Making the beam brighter with more electrons
Using a screen that is much larger
b.why: The crystal diffracts electrons well only when their wavelength is close to the spacing of its atoms. A much shorter wavelength would diffract even less. More electrons or a bigger screen does not change how the waves spread.
b.clue: Diffraction needs the wavelength to match the size of the gaps.

b.best: Using electrons with a wavelength near the atom spacing

The right option is the only one with a qualifier ('can behave'), and the distractors are obviously false (faster than light, no charge, heavier than atoms), so the answer is easy to spot without knowing the idea.

b.q: Nina fires electrons at a thin crystal and sees only a single bright spot straight ahead, with no rings. Which change would most likely bring the rings back?
opts: Slowing the electrons so each has a longer wavelength
Speeding the electrons up so each has a shorter wavelength
Sending more electrons at the crystal each second
Sending fewer electrons at the crystal each second
b.why: The spot means the spread is too small to see, so the wavelength is much smaller than the atom spacing. Slower electrons have a longer wavelength, which spreads more and can bring the rings back. A shorter wavelength spreads even less, and the number of electrons does not change the spread.
b.clue: What does the amount of spreading depend on, and which way must it change?

b.best: Slowing the electrons so each has a longer wavelength
